The answer to most questions that try to relate quantum concepts to classical concepts is: "Kind of but not really."

What's important to understand is the concept of uncertainty. A particle never has a perfectly well-defined location, it's always spread out over space. And particles tend to get spread out as much as they can, really. This is what that looks like. This shows the probability distribution of finding a particle at any point in space. You see that it's moving to the right and getting more and more spread out as it moves along.

If you were to try to "find" (localize) the particle, it would snap into one certain position. Not necessarily at the center of the distribution, but near the center is the most likely location it will end up at.

Now if you stick a particle in a trap, it will creep around and "leak out" of it a bit. It will be mostly inside, but the wave function will trail off out of the trap slightly. The stronger the trap, the less this happens. If you try to localize the particle then, you're most likely to find it inside the trap, but there will be a small but non-zero probability of finding it outside. That's what we refer to as "tunneling".

That's a very good question that nobody has a good answer to yet!

There are three generations of quarks (up/down, charm/strange, top/bottom) and three generations of leptons (electron/electron neutrino, muon/muon neutrino, tau/tau neutrino). The third generation is heavier than the second, which is heavier than the first, which is also how they decay. This seems very suggestive of some underlying mechanism that causes both to have these three generations, but so far all attempts at finding one have failed.

The half-integer spin actually has nothing to do with thirds. The fact that quarks have fractional charge is in itself really weird. The Standard Model of particle physics is really great at describing how these particles interact with each other, but we don't really understand why we have the ones we have and what causes their properties.
